I'm fairly unfamiliar with software engineering, can you give me an idea what your curriculum focused on?

Well, the pithy answer is "See this website we're on right now? I make things like this". But more generally:

In university I got a shiny B.Sc in Computer Science. It split pretty evenly half-and-half theory and practice. Theory courses concerned the various academic subjects relevant to software. These were things like

  • Data structures and algorithms analysis. Common solutions to common problems and their time/space tradeoffs. The attendant (discrete) math and statistics needed to make sense of this
  • Operating systems. How To Unix 101. The various concepts behind operating systems and related concepts. Academic things like scheduling, a little bit of cybernetics/control systems, workflow management. Practical, real-world-dependent things such as the tricks computers use to manage memory, enhance performance, communicate with each other, etc
  • Automata theory, which is best described as "extreme flowcharting". The various classes of automata, how they map to different languages ( see Chomsky Hierarchy), and the mathematical implications. Godel Escher Bach stuff. I know regular expressions now
  • AI and AI concepts. Neural nets, expert systems, logic programming, etc
  • Networking and networking concepts. Lots of graph traversal algorithms and statistical analysis
  • Bioinformatics (DS/Algos applied to biology problems. DNA is the biggest of big data in many ways)
  • Cryptography and attendant mathematics. Which I couldn't tell you anything about, because the first ten rules of crypto are "DON'T DO IT YOURSELF"

Practical things were things like

  • Courses in various programming languages (Java, C, C++, Ruby, Javascript, Prolog)
  • Courses in object orientation: how to sanely structure large codebases
  • Lower level processor details (I wrote an emulator for a toy processor)
  • Rudimentary project management training, specifically around Scrum/XP/Agile methodologies
  • How to make website. Perl CGI, PHP, Javascript

In my day to day job, most of my responsibilities are the same as any engineer in any other discipline. I spend most of my day doing two things. First, I talk to "customers" (internal product managers and other technical team leads), trying to understand what they need and figure out the best way to solve their problems. Second, I talk to teammates about how to best engineer a solution. The solution is almost but not always 'writing software' (sometimes it's 'using this software thing someone else wrote', rarely it's 'that's a dumb thing, we're not doing it', and every once in a while it's "we can totally already do that").

As I'm primarily a web developer, writing software usually means it's in the Ruby on Rails framework, following their design decisions and best practices. Our website's primary role is to expose relevant business data to customers and allow them to manage it, and so a lot of the actual 'features' are exposing complicated data models and workflows to end users in ways that aren't confusing. Imagine the profile management page of any website, for instance.

As I work on a large, old codebase, a disproportionate amount of my time is spent doing exploratory programming. Our codebase does a lot of things, it has a lot of quirks, and almost all of the original authors have since moved on. Often my job involves figuring out what exactly our code does, how and why. This is usually done in the service of fixing some customer-facing bug, and usually reveals deep-seated architectural problems. The best real-engineering example I can think of is: imagine that we didn't hear about the new Bay Bridge's problems until 10 years from now. You're brought in to figure out the what-how-why. What exactly is the problem? How is it happening/how do we fix it. Why did it happen. We know the bay bridge rods are breaking because of improper storage during construction. But what if we didn't find breaking rods until 2025. The construction workers have long since moved on, so it would be difficult to figure out what part of their process broke the bridge. Figuring that out (or the software equivalent) is what I mean by exploratory programming.

There's a lot of extremely complex work that goes into powering seemingly simple things. A lot of this is simply the momentum of a decade of inelegant decisions. I'd call them 'bad', but they're only bad from Engineering's PoV; they have good business reasons for existing. Add to that people management: once you figure out why it takes 4 hours to change two lines of text on one web page, you have to communicate that to nontechnical management in a way that doesn't make them think "eqdw is an idiot" is the cause of the problem.

At the end of the day, the work I do appears simplistic and boring. As an example, here's a list of all the things I've accomplished since March. For context: I work at a company whose primary product is on-demand book printing and the software tools to facilitate that

  • Make our admin tools show what shipping service tier users used on an order, when they're sending a user a free reprint order. Previously, they would have to look at a separate page to figure it out, and then select it from a list on the reprint page
  • Fix a bug where validations were failing in the administrative back end, because two lists of the same elements in different order are not considered equal
  • Automating the processing of sales data given to us from a distribution partner. They send us spreadsheet files and I wrote code to convert those into meaningful data objects in the accounting part of our database.
  • Fixing a weird edge case in our volume order workflow (if you want economies of scale, you can pre-order a thousand books, we'll hold them in inventory, and you drive your per-unit cost down substantially)
  • Identified code that exists in our codebase but isn't used anywhere, and deleted it
  • Deleted a bunch of old tests that are no longer valid, and upgraded some others into our new modern testing library
  • Wrote a small software client to let us more conveniently use an internal web service that another team wrote
  • Fix a billion edge cases where PDFs are treated the same as physical books but they aren't physical books and this causes bugs
  • Wrote code to deal with the situation where you're looking at book edit histories that are so old that they used a different, incompatible-with-present data model.
  • Fixed a really complicated twelve-step infinite loop that occurs when you try to delete a book that has been converted into a pdf (see "fix a billion edge cases").
